Hotel-to-hostel conversions in Hong Kong mark the birth of a genuine asset class
article:
From 2020 until recently, Hong Kong was a hard sell. Its borders stayed largely shut through the pandemic, and travel with mainland China did not fully resume until Feb 6, 2023.

Interest rates climbed, and the city’s property market went through a six-year correction that began in late 2019, driving down the values of offices, retail properties and warehouses. Today, capital is returning to Hong Kong, and one of the clearest signals is coming from an unlikely sector: student accommodation.

Hong Kong has set out to become Asia’s education hub, but its universities now admit more students from overseas and mainland China than they can house. To fill the gap, investors are buying hotels built for tourists and turning them into student hostels. Singapore’s CapitaLand Investment is among those pursuing the opportunity, with a proposed HK$2.3 billion ($380 million) deal for one such hotel.

Our view is simple: Student housing in Hong Kong has the makings of a lasting asset class, not just a passing trade. But what is driving the rush of capital, what returns can investors realistically expect, and where should they exercise caution?

Why investors stayed away

Before I get to why student beds are suddenly in demand, it helps to rewind a little. Why did so many investors walk away from Hong Kong in the first place?

Office values fell by about half from their 2018 peaks, while retail values declined by around 42%. Financing also became harder to secure. A CBRE survey ranked Hong Kong as the toughest major market in the region for raising property debt, while lending across Asia Pacific, excluding Japan, fell to a 16-year low in the first half of 2026. For many investors, sitting on the sidelines was the easier choice.

Hotels had problems of their own. Tourists returned, with 49.9 million arrivals in 2025. But they spent less than they used to. Overnight visitors spent HK$5,503 each in 2025, down from HK$6,614 in 2018. Day-trippers spent roughly half what they did before, while hotel room rates also came under pressure.

According to CBRE, average hotel room rates fell 11% y-o-y in early 2025.

For hotel owners, the search for a more reliable source of income was becoming increasingly urgent. As it turned out, another sector was facing a very different problem: demand was growing faster than supply.

Study, stay, work

Hong Kong wants to attract young talent and keep it. In September 2025, the Hong Kong government announced that the non-local student quota at publicly funded universities would rise from 40% to 50% from the 2026/2027 academic year.

The pitch is simple: Come to Hong Kong to study, then stay on to work. We regard this as one of the more coherent approaches to talent recruitment and retention in the region. It also gives the student accommodation sector a source of demand that does not depend on a recovery in the office market.

Hong Kong’s universities provide another draw. In the QS World University Rankings 2027, published in June 2026, the University of Hong Kong was placed 11th and the Chinese University of Hong Kong 18th. It was the first time two Hong Kong universities had ranked among the world’s top 20.

This year, Hong Kong overtook the US as the second most popular overseas study destination for students from mainland China. Hong Kong approved more than 94,500 student visas last year, more than double the number in 2022, according to an August 2026 article by Propmodo.

The challenge is finding accommodation for these students, as the supply of beds has failed to keep pace with demand.

Hong Kong had about 192,000 university students in the 2024/2025 academic year, but only around 44,000 hostel beds. That works out to more than four students for every bed, although not all students require hostel accommodation, and estimates of the actual shortfall vary. Savills puts the gap at around 88,000 beds, while JLL estimates a shortage of 76,300 beds in 2026, widening to 147,200 by the 2029/2030 academic year.

Regardless of the methodology, the shortfall is substantial. Private purpose-built student accommodation (PBSA) has barely made a dent in the shortage, with only about 6,900 beds currently available and another 16,300 in the pipeline.

Rents tell a similar story. According to JLL, stabilised rents range from HK$7,000 to HK$10,000 per bed per month, or approximately $1,150 to $1,650. Student accommodation rents in Hong Kong have risen by 10% annually since 2022, while major developments are reporting occupancy rates of 98% to 100%.

Such strong demand has not gone unnoticed by investors.

When hotels become hostels

In July 2025, the Hong Kong government introduced the Hostels in the City Scheme, making it easier to convert hotels and other commercial properties into student accommodation.

To us, this is what good policy design looks like: removing regulatory obstacles rather than simply handing out subsidies. If demand is the fuel, the scheme provides the spark.

Under the Hostels in the City Scheme, a hotel converted into student accommodation remains classified as non-domestic. Owners can therefore avoid the lengthy rezoning and floor-area cuts that a switch to residential use would normally bring. In most cases, there is also no change to the land lease and no extra land premium to pay, potentially avoiding one of the biggest costs in a Hong Kong redevelopment.

The owners moved fast. By February 2026, the scheme had 25 applications covering about 5,100 beds. By September, 41 applications covering around 10,800 beds had been deemed eligible, reflecting the pace of investor interest.

Hotels led the way because they could be converted relatively quickly. They were already configured as rows of small rooms, and conversions typically take two to six months, compared with six to 18 months for offices. Faster conversion means rental income can begin flowing sooner.

What strikes us most is not the pace but the breadth of the buyer pool. In March, China Resources Longdation, part of a mainland state-owned group, paid HK$953 million for Hotel COZi Oasis in Kwai Chung, which will hold about 900 beds.

That same month, Centaline, best known as one of the city’s biggest property agencies, bought the 494-room Regal Oriental for HK$1.52 billion. Banks subsequently competed for a HK$1 billion financing mandate for its conversion.

Local developer Wang On teamed up with US private equity firm Angelo Gordon on Sunny House, a 720-unit conversion that is currently 98% occupied. In September, Singapore’s CapitaLand Investment moved to buy the 550-room ibis Hong Kong Central & Sheung Wan for HK$2.3 billion, one of the largest bets on the sector yet.

For such a young sector, the breadth of capital flowing in is striking. Mainland Chinese state-owned groups, local property agencies and banks, US private equity firms, and now one of Singapore’s largest real estate managers are pursuing opportunities in the same market.

But with so much money chasing these assets, the obvious question is: What kind of returns can investors actually expect?

What investors can expect

The answer depends very much on the asset. Industry estimates provide a useful benchmark, but they are no guarantee of actual returns.

JLL’s research estimates that office-to-student accommodation conversions could achieve target internal rates of return of 15% to 18% over a five-year holding period, compared with 13% to 16% for hotel conversions. These are target returns, however, and actual performance will depend on rental income, occupancy rates, operating costs and the eventual sale price.

Much of the appeal lies in the nature of the income. Nick Tang, CEO and executive director of Wang On, describes student housing as offering “stable and predictable income”.

Lenders appear to recognise that appeal, too. Bank of China (Hong Kong), for instance, reportedly competed against Industrial Bank’s Hong Kong branch and other lenders for the HK$1 billion loan mandate for the Regal Oriental conversion.

When banks compete to lend in a market where property financing is otherwise difficult to secure, it tells us they see something attractive in the underlying income. I think that is significant. But the competition for selected deals should not be mistaken for a broader recovery in property lending.

The UK offers a glimpse of what a mature student housing market looks like. Investors poured GBP2.1 billion ($3.56 billion) into UK PBSA in the first quarter of 2026 alone. Knight Frank puts prime London net initial yields at around 4.5%, compared with 5.25% to 5.5% in regional markets.

Hong Kong is still some way from that level of market maturity. That early stage is part of the appeal. It is also where much of the risk lies.

The risk of arriving late

Every property boom eventually reaches a point where early investors have made their money and latecomers risk paying too much. Hong Kong’s student housing market may not be there yet, but the warning signs are worth watching.

The first is price. Colliers senior director of hotel advisory Shaman Chellaram has cautioned that the remaining opportunity is “diminishing quite quickly” as more capital pours into the sector. More bidders mean higher acquisition prices, and higher entry costs mean thinner returns.

Then there is the question of how much demand each property can realistically capture. The citywide shortage is real, but so is the rush to fill it.

A shortage across Hong Kong does not mean every building will benefit equally. Students generally prefer to live near campus, and accommodation an hour away is a harder sell.

The pipeline of 16,300 beds is more than double the existing purpose-built supply. Even developers acknowledge “a real probability of oversupply in the next few years”. Oversupply in the wrong locations and scarcity in the right ones can easily co-exist.

Then there is policy risk. Much of the increase in demand has been driven by Hong Kong’s decision to admit more non-local students, alongside mainland Chinese families increasingly viewing the city as an alternative to the US.

But policies change, and so do family choices. If either shifts, the flow of incoming students could slow.

I do not expect demand to reverse, but I would be cautious about assuming today’s rental growth and occupancy rates will continue indefinitely. In a more crowded market, realised returns could drift towards the lower end of expectations, with a widening gap between winners and losers.

This is an operating business

If there is one point I want investors to take away, it is this: Owning student housing is closer to running a business than simply collecting rent.

Rooms turn over every academic year, so occupancy must be rebuilt annually.

Student welfare, community, safety and university relationships all influence whether beds are filled at the projected rents. In mature markets, the difference between strong and weak operators is reflected directly in net operating income.

In Hong Kong, where the sector is still young and operating track records are limited, I believe choosing the right operator may be just as important as choosing the right building, if not more so.

Prudent investors should therefore test whether their investments remain viable if rental growth slows, occupancy falls or operating costs rise. Stability is the product of good operations. It does not come with the title deed.

The Hostels in the City Scheme also comes with restrictions. Converted properties must reserve at least 90% of their places for eligible students, limiting operators’ flexibility to accommodate other tenants if student demand weakens.

That restriction does not undermine the investment case, but it is another reminder that these assets cannot simply be treated as conventional rental properties.

The real test is the exit

The exit matters as much as the entry. Yet while much of the market is focused on getting in, I am more interested in the exit.

According to Real Estate Asia, buyers today are predominantly family offices, private investors, private equity funds and state-owned enterprises. Pension funds, insurers and sovereign wealth funds are expected to follow, but only once assets have matured and established a track record.

That institutional participation could ultimately broaden the buyer pool, improve liquidity and help establish long-term pricing for the asset class.

Hong Kong is still at the beginning of that journey. If it follows even part of the UK’s path, early investors holding well-located, professionally managed and stabilised assets could benefit as institutional capital enters the market and yields compress.

If that institutional demand fails to materialise, however, investors could find themselves holding an operating business with a limited pool of potential buyers, in a market where refinancing remains difficult.

For anyone buying today, the eventual sale may depend on whether larger institutional investors are willing to pay for the income stream that has been built.

That is why asset selection matters so much. Institutions typically seek assets with proven operating histories, and building that track record takes years of sustained occupancy and reliable income.

The properties that institutional investors may eventually want to own are being selected, developed and operated today. Not every hostel will make the cut.

What Singapore investors should take from this

For Singapore investors, student housing offers a way to participate in Hong Kong’s recovery without betting on a rebound in offices or retail.

Hong Kong’s hotels were built for a city of tourists. Many are now being repurposed for a growing population of students. That shift says something about the city’s ability to adapt its existing real estate to changing demand.

The timing is worth noting. CapitaLand’s move shows that major Singapore investors are no longer merely watching this emerging sector from the sidelines.

Hong Kong is close and familiar, and its property market has been through years of repricing. Student housing offers exposure to a different source of demand, supported by the city’s education policies, internationally ranked universities and shortage of accommodation.

With more capital chasing opportunities in the sector, investors will need to be increasingly selective. Location matters, particularly proximity to universities and transport links. So does the track record of the operator, and whether the acquisition price still makes financial sense if rental growth slows or stalls.

I believe student housing has the makings of a lasting asset class, not a passing investment trend. But not every conversion will succeed, nor will every investor achieve the returns being projected. Those who do best will need conviction and discipline in equal measure.

For much of the past five years, the question was whether Hong Kong was worth the risk at all.

Today, the question is narrower and more useful: Which beds, where, and at what price?

Investors who answer that carefully may find that one of Hong Kong’s newest asset classes becomes one of its most enduring investment opportunities.

title: Thomson Reserve: First mega launch in eight years at Upper Thomson, priced from $2,608 psf
article:
The 1,268-unit Thomson Reserve will be the largest new private residential project to launch in Singapore this year, and the first mega development with more than 1,000 units to debut in 2026.

Occupying a sprawling 5ha site — equivalent to about seven football fields — the development has a prominent 500m frontage along Upper Thomson Road.

A VIP preview will be held on Friday, Oct 16, ahead of the public preview the following day. The official launch is scheduled for Oct 31.

It will be the first major new residential launch in the Upper Thomson–Shunfu neighbourhood in eight years, following the 1,206-unit JadeScape in 2018.

The 99-year leasehold Thomson Reserve is a redevelopment of the former Thomson View Condominium , which was sold en bloc for $810 million in November 2024.

The buyer was a consortium comprising CapitaLand Development (CLD), with a 50% stake, UOL Group (40%) and its subsidiary, Singapore Land Group (10%).

The acquisition marked the end of a 17-year collective-sale journey for Thomson View’s owners, who had made five attempts since 2007 before finally securing a buyer.

The $810 million purchase price translated into a land rate of $1,178 psf per plot ratio (psf ppr), after factoring in the land betterment charges and the lease top-up premium to a fresh 99 years.

“Land acquisition cost is naturally an important consideration in any development, particularly one of this scale,” says UOL Group CEO Liam Wee Sin.

“However, we also have to assess the overall development potential and economics of a site. At Thomson Reserve, we saw an opportunity to leverage the scale and natural attributes of the site to deliver a differentiated residential experience.”

Proximity to nature and amenities

Thomson Reserve is surrounded by established low-rise private residential estates, including Soo Chow Gardens and Adelphi Park, as well as Windsor Park Estate , which is a Good Class Bungalow area.

Its elevated position offers panoramic views stretching from the surrounding landed estates to the city skyline, Singapore Island Country Club, Windsor Nature Park, the Central Catchment Nature Reserve and Bukit Timah Nature Reserve.

The Central Catchment Nature Reserve spans more than 3,000ha of forests and reservoirs, including MacRitchie Reservoir and Upper and Lower Peirce Reservoirs.

“What made this particular site especially compelling is also its scale and permanent natural setting,” says Liam. “The elevated topography, surrounding landed housing enclaves and proximity to the reservoirs and Central Catchment offer exceptional views and a sense of openness that is increasingly rare in Singapore.”

The development is a two-minute walk from Upper Thomson MRT Station on the Thomson-East Coast Line, with sheltered access from the main entrance.

Ai Tong School is within walking distance, while Thomson Plaza is directly across Upper Thomson Road and accessible via an overhead bridge or the MRT station’s underground linkway.

Residents will also have access to the popular Upper Thomson dining stretch, which includes longstanding eateries such as Casuarina Curry, Nam Kee Chicken Rice and The Roti Prata House, alongside establishments such as Columbus Coffee Co, Filo Bistro, Salted Caramel and Omoté.

“Redeveloping [the Thomson View] site has given us an opportunity to build on the strengths of an established neighbourhood,” says CLD CEO (Singapore & International) Ronald Tay.

Two collections catering to different buyers

Thomson Reserve comprises two residential collections. The Classic Collection has 740 units across four 21-storey towers, while the Luxury Collection comprises 528 units in two 30-storey towers.

The Classic Collection offers two- to four-bedroom layouts, while the Luxury Collection features a mix of two-bedroom premium units to five-bedroom suites. Of the 528 units in the Luxury Collection, 112 larger four-bedroom premium units and five-bedroom suites feature private lift access.

Two-bedroom configurations make up  716 units (56.5%). Unit sizes range from 592 to 775 sq ft, with prices starting from $1.544 million ($2,608 psf).

Three-bedroom unit types account for another 350 units (27.6%), with sizes ranging from 947 to 1,152 sq ft. Prices start from $2.503 million ($2,643 psf).

Four-bedroom units account for 174 units (13.7%), ranging from 1,238 to 1,485 sq ft. Prices start from $3.388 million ($2,737 psf) for a 1,238 sq ft apartment.

At the top end are 28 five-bedroom suites, each measuring 1,808 sq ft. Occupying a single residential stack with unblocked views towards MacRitchie Reservoir and the Orchard Road skyline, they account for just 2.2% of the development.

The range of apartment sizes is intended to appeal to buyers at different stages of life. “While we expect interest from buyers familiar with the Upper Thomson neighbourhood, we believe its appeal extends beyond the immediate catchment to homebuyers across Singapore,” says CLD’s Tay.

He expects Thomson Reserve to attract first-time homeowners, young families and HDB upgraders, as well as existing private homeowners looking to upgrade or rightsize, and multigenerational families seeking larger living spaces.

Bringing the Central Catchment  into the development

The six residential towers occupy just 12% of Thomson Reserve’s site, leaving the remaining 88% for landscaping, water features and recreational facilities.

Designed by P&T Consultants, the towers have been oriented to maximise views of the surrounding greenery and minimise direct overlooking between blocks.

Inspired by the man-made contours of nearby MacRitchie Reservoir, P&T designed organically shaped pools and water features across the grounds to evoke a series of mini reservoirs. More than 45% of the residential stacks face the Central Catchment Nature Reserve, while over 80% enjoy either greenery views or views of the development’s internal landscaping and waterscapes designed by Ecoplan Asia.

The development will have more than 80 facilities across three clubhouses, including eight swimming pools, two of which are 50m lap pools.

“Situated on one of the largest collective sale sites in recent history, the generous land size has allowed the developers to curate expansive greenery and comprehensive facilities,” says Mark Yip, CEO of Huttons Asia, one of the three appointed joint marketing agents for Thomson Reserve, alongside PropNex and ERA.

Marcus Chu, CEO of ERA Singapore, believes the development’s elevated position and surrounding views will appeal particularly to buyers of higher-floor apartments. However, he considers the combination of greenery and convenience to be the stronger draw.

“Views may influence which unit a buyer chooses, but location and liveability are more likely to drive the decision to choose the development in the first place,” he says. Thomson Reserve is expected to obtain its temporary occupation permit in the second half of 2030.  Pent-up demand for new homes.

The last mega condo launch in the immediate Upper Thomson–Shunfu area was JadeScape in 2018. Developed by Qingjian Realty, the project occupies the former Shunfu Ville site, a privatised HUDC estate that the developer acquired through an en bloc sale for $638 million in 2016.

JadeScape was subsequently fully sold and completed in 2022.

“Thomson Reserve represents the first new mega development of more than 1,000 units to be launched in the Bishan Planning Area in about eight years,” says Mohan Sandrasegeran, SRI’s head of research and data analytics.

It will be the UOL-CapitaLand joint venture’s second mega development in two years, following the 1,193-unit ParkTown Residence in Tampines. Launched in February 2025, ParkTown Residence sold 1,041 units, or 87%, during its launch weekend and is now 98% sold.

“We expect Thomson Reserve to garner healthy buyer interest owing partly to pent-up demand, its strong location attributes, and the wide selection of units at the development,” says Kelvin Fong, CEO of PropNex.

Mega developments tend to attract interest because of their wider range of unit types, greater market visibility and extensive recreational facilities, Fong adds. For prospective buyers at Thomson Reserve, JadeScape also offers a useful pricing benchmark. Both are large 99-year leasehold developments in District 20, near MRT stations, and are redevelopments of private sites purchased en bloc.

According to ERA Research and Market Intelligence, JadeScape’s median resale price reached $2,341 psf in 2026, up 7.6% from 2023, based on caveats lodged as at Oct 13.

Meanwhile, SRI Research’s analysis of URA Realis caveats showed 253 resale transactions at JadeScape to date. All 253 transactions recorded gross gains for their respective sellers, based on the difference between their recorded purchase and resale prices, says Sandrasegeran.

Where will buyers come from?

PropNex’s sales data from JadeScape’s launch in 2018 and subsequent sales showed that about 53% of buyers served by the agency had HDB addresses. At the 372-unit Amo Residence , launched in 2022, the corresponding proportion was 46%. At both projects, just over a quarter of buyers served by PropNex lived in District 20.

“These figures suggest that new launches in the area can draw demand from a meaningful pool of HDB upgraders, as well as buyers already living in the district,” says PropNex’s Fong.

He expects HDB upgraders at Thomson Reserve to come from established estates such as Bishan and Ang Mo Kio, with interest likely to be concentrated in the larger two-bedroom and three-bedroom units.

Bishan recorded 79 HDB resale transactions of at least $1 million as at Oct 13, compared with 98 for the whole of 2025, according to ERA Research and Market Intelligence.

Another potential buyer group is landed homeowners looking to rightsize. ERA data shows that the median resale price of landed homes in District 20 has almost doubled from $1,152 psf in 2016 to $2,300 psf in the first nine months of 2026. This appreciation could allow owners to unlock some of their housing equity while remaining in a familiar neighbourhood, says ERA’s Chu.

He also sees potential demand for two-bedroom units from singles who want to live near their parents in the surrounding landed estates. “This allows families to stay connected while maintaining their own living space,” he says.

Larger three- to five-bedroom apartments, meanwhile, are expected to attract families seeking more space, while investors could be drawn by the development’s MRT connectivity and rental potential.

Huttons’ Yip estimates that existing private homeowners could account for about 80% of buyers at Thomson Reserve, with HDB upgraders making up the remaining 20%.

Rising land costs put future prices in focus

Beyond the resale market, the outcome of a recent Government Land Sale (GLS) tender in the neighbourhood provides another reference point for Thomson Reserve’s pricing.

The Lorong Puntong–Sin Ming Avenue residential site attracted seven bids when its tender closed on Sept 15. Malaysian developer Eco World Development submitted the highest offer of $208.1 million, or $1,612 psf ppr.

“The Lorong Puntong–Sin Ming Avenue GLS site tender is particularly interesting, as it gives us a glimpse of what developers are prepared to pay for future residential supply in this neighbourhood,” says ERA’s Chu. At $1,612 psf ppr, Eco World’s bid was approximately 37% higher than the $1,178 psf ppr land rate for the former Thomson View site. “This does not mean future selling prices will be 37% higher,” Chu says. “It suggests that the replacement cost of new homes in the Thomson-Bishan area is rising.”

With prices starting from $2,608 psf and a broad mix of two- to five-bedroom homes, Thomson Reserve will test buyers’ willingness to pay for a new home in one of Singapore’s established residential enclaves. Its appeal rests on a combination of connectivity, spacious homes, and views of the surrounding greenery.

One of these, a published Phase 1 study in eight healthy male participants reported absolute bioavailability of approximately 29% for a 25mg sublingual ketamine wafer.

This study shows that the wafer can deliver ketamine rapidly. While clinical data are most advanced for Wafermine® and other formulations remain at earlier stages, this human evidence reduces platform risk relative to a technology supported only by laboratory testing.

title: Hidden Gems: 3 Cash-Rich SGX Stocks Raising Dividends as Rates Stay High

Look at

Why does that matter?

Is Info-Tech’s dividend increase backed by cash?
Info-Tech Systems Ltd (SGX: ITS) sells cloud-based software for human resource management, accounting and customer relationship management, and runs AI training through Info-Tech Academy.
For 1H2026, revenue rose 22% year on year (YoY) to S$27.3 million.
Subscriptions, which make up the bulk of sales, grew 12% to S$21.2 million.
Services revenue rose 116% to S$4.9 million on demand for the group’s AI training.
Profit attributable to owners rose 89% to S$9.7 million, though two one-offs flattered it.
Info-Tech received a S$1 million Enterprise Singapore grant in January 2026, and the 1H2025 figure included roughly S$2 million in listing expenses.
Strip out these one-offs and the company puts adjusted profit after tax at S$8.7 million, a more modest 20% increase.
Free cash flow climbed to S$15.1 million from S$6.2 million, and a S$6.9 million release from trade receivables gave it a lift.
Even without that boost, free cash flow would have covered the S$4.3 million interim dividend bill nearly twice over.
The interim dividend rose 8.4% to S$0.0168 per share, which the company says amounts to 45% of net profit.
Info-Tech ended June with S$76.6 million in cash and no borrowings, against S$5.1 million in lease liabilities.
The catch? Info-Tech listed only in July 2025, so its dividend record is short.
Part of its growth also hinges on AI training, which management expects Singapore’s SkillsFuture initiatives to support.

Why did China Sunsine double its dividend while free cash flow fell?
China Sunsine Chemical Holdings Ltd
(SGX: QES) makes rubber chemicals in China for tyre makers including Bridgestone and Pirelli.
Revenue for 1H2026 rose 19% YoY to RMB 2 billion as its average selling price and sales volume each climbed 9%.
Sunsine sold a record 119,959 tonnes.
Gross margin widened from 24.6% to 25.2%, and gross profit grew 22% to RMB 506.0 million.
Net profit attributable to shareholders rose a slower 5% to RMB 254.3 million.
A stronger renminbi against the US dollar led to RMB 47.8 million in net other losses, and administrative and research costs also rose.
Free cash flow fell about 91% to RMB 25.4 million from RMB 280.5 million because Sunsine tied up more cash in inventories and trade receivables.
A cut in capital expenditure, to RMB 51.6 million from RMB 151.0 million, softened the blow.
What pays for a doubled dividend? The
balance sheet
.
Sunsine held RMB 2.2 billion in cash and no borrowings as at 30 June 2026, more than eight times its half-year profit.
Its interim dividend doubled to S$0.01 per share.
High raw material prices and domestic oversupply persist, so management will keep balancing sales with production.
A 20,000-tonne project at its Weifang plant should begin commercial production by end-2026 and is expected to lift annual capacity to 272,000 tonnes.
Sunsine will need to find buyers for that extra output.

Can Delfi keep raising its dividend as margins shrink?
Delfi Ltd
(SGX: P34) is best known for its SilverQueen, Ceres and Delfi chocolate brands in Indonesia, and sells consumer products across 17 markets.
Revenue for 1H2026 rose 2.7% YoY to US$266.6 million.
Own Brands sales grew 13.3%, but Agency Brands sales fell 12.4% after an agency account ended in the third quarter of 2025.
Profit attributable to shareholders increased 5.4% to US$12.9 million.
A US$2.6 million net foreign exchange gain and a 14% drop in tax expense propped up that figure.
Higher raw material costs and weaker regional currencies squeezed gross margin by 1.8 percentage points to 25.7%, and EBITDA fell 3.7% to US$23.4 million.
Free cash flow fell about 81% to US$10.1 million from US$52.2 million.
Lower advertising and promotion accruals and heavier payments to suppliers drove most of that drop.
Delfi held US$63.3 million in cash against US$20.3 million as at 30 June 2026, for net cash of US$43.0 million.
Its interim dividend rose 4.7% to S$0.0134 per share, the smallest increase of the three.
Management expects cocoa prices to stay volatile and the Middle East conflict to push up operating costs.
Related articles:
Beyond STI: 3 Cash-Heavy Stocks Paying More Than Your CPF
June 2026 Watchlist: 3 Small-Cap SGX Stocks for Retirement Income
Get Smart: Find out what drained the cash
A sharp fall in free cash flow does not doom a dividend.
What matters is why the cash fell.
Cash tied up in inventories, receivables or supplier payments can flow back in later periods.
Sunsine’s shortfall came largely from working capital in a half when its gross profit grew 22%.
Delfi’s drop was also mostly working capital, though its thinner gross margin is a separate squeeze on earnings.
The next time a company raises its dividend in a weak cash half, ask yourself whether that cash will come back.
For Sunsine and Delfi, watch free cash flow when they report full-year results.

article:

DPU rose 11.3% year on year to S$0.05714, while distributable income grew even faster, up 18.5% to S$150.7 million.

Positive rental reversions and escalations lifted income.
The REIT also bought Tokyo Data Centre 3 and, in February 2026, completed its purchase of the remaining interests in Keppel DC Singapore 3 and 4.
But that’s only part of the story.
Where is the growth coming from?
Demand for data centres is still the main engine.
The REIT manager points to forecasts that global data centre capacity will grow 25% a year to reach 256 GW by 2030.
What’s holding back the new supply isn’t money.
It’s power.
According to Keppel DC REIT, the hardest part of building a data centre is securing enough electricity and a grid connection, then winning planning approval.
These hurdles are steepest in established “Tier 1” markets such as Singapore, Japan and the major European hubs, where land and power are in short supply.
That scarcity plays to Keppel DC REIT’s strengths.
The REIT already owns operating data centres in exactly these markets, and clients have contracted around 95% of the power capacity it can earn revenue from.
How is Keppel DC REIT paying for its growth?
With more debt, though on better terms than a year ago:
Average cost of debt fell to 2.6% in 1H 2026 from 3.0% a year ago.
Interest cover rose to 6.9 times from 5.9 times.
Fixed-rate debt rose to 87% of borrowings from 76%.
A bigger debt load still costs more.
Total borrowings grew from S$1.6 billion in 1H 2025 to around S$2.3 billion in 1H 2026, and finance costs climbed 25.2% year on year to S$30.7 million.
Gearing rose to 34% from 30%.
In short, Keppel DC REIT is carrying more debt at a lower
interest rate
.
That trade-off works as long as the newly acquired assets earn more than they cost, and net property income (NPI) growth of 15.1% to S$210.4 million suggests they do.
What are the risks?
Internet enterprise clients, mostly hyperscalers, accounted for 70.4% of rental income as of 30 June 2026, up from 67.4% a year earlier.
Here’s the rub: Keppel DC REIT’s single largest client contributes 43.5%.
This concentration cuts both ways.
Hyperscalers generally have higher credit quality and give investors direct exposure to AI-driven demand.
Unfortunately, Keppel DC REIT has not named its largest client.
Meanwhile, portfolio occupancy slipped to 92.5% in 1H 2026 from 95.8% a year ago.
Almost all of the decline comes from Cardiff Data Centre, whose contract expired in June 2026 and which now sits vacant.
Strip Cardiff out and portfolio occupancy would be 95.3%.
A few other assets still need work.
Keppel DC Singapore 1 remains at 46.5% occupancy after the non-renewal of its non-data-centre space, which makes up a significant portion of the asset.
The sale of Basis Bay, which has 40.2% occupancy, is taking longer than expected.
Keppel DC REIT announced the divestment on 2 January 2025 and had targeted completion by 3Q 2025.
In Guangdong, the manager has committed to no significant capital expenditure on its troubled data centres as it explores exit options.

Top 4 S-REITs Raising DPU by 10% or More
The “Data Centre” Gold Mine: Keppel DC REIT vs. Digital Core REIT
Get Smart: Follow the rent back to who pays it
Keppel DC REIT owns data centres in markets where power limits new supply, and that position supports its growth.
A distribution, though, is only as dependable as the tenants who pay the rent.
When one client contributes 43.5%, that client’s financial health matters as much as the industry’s growth.
So before you weigh up any REIT’s DPU growth, ask yourself: how much of the rent comes from the biggest tenant, and how confident are you that it will keep paying?
The answer may give you a clue as to whether you should buy the REIT.

title: IMF sees Asia’s growth slowing despite AI-fuelled resilience
article:
(Oct 15): The International Monetary Fund expects economic growth in the Asia-Pacific to slow this year and next, warning that rising energy prices and any pullback in the artificial-intelligence boom could test the region’s resilience.

Growth in the Asia-Pacific is projected at 4.8% in 2026, down from 5% last year but above the IMF’s April forecast of 4.4%. This will further moderate to 4.4% in 2027, the Washington-based fund said in its October regional economic outlook report.

The IMF raised its growth forecasts for most advanced economies, with projections revised up “sizably” for the likes of South Korea, Taiwan and Hong Kong that are reaping the benefits of the AI-driven investments surge. It also upgraded its outlook for China and India, while lowering predictions for countries facing higher inflation without comparable gains from technology demand.

The revisions highlight how strong demand for semiconductors, data centers and related technology products has helped cushion parts of Asia against mounting economic pressures. But the gains have been uneven, concentrated in economies plugged into global technology supply chains, the IMF said.

“Think of countries like Bangladesh, Cambodia, Laos, all these countries are importing oil. They are not benefiting from the AI boom that much. So these countries are a lot more vulnerable and they also have fewer policy buffers,” said Krishna Srinivasan, director of the IMF’s Asia and Pacific Department, in an interview with Bloomberg, adding that economies exposed to energy shocks but less integrated into global supply chains face greater risks.

See also: ECB may not have to do as much if markets tighten, Dolenc says

Some countries in Asia are already beginning to factor in a moderation in the AI tech cycle. Singapore’s central bank is expecting the boom to ease in latter half of 2027, following broader concerns from global policymakers about the sustainability of the trillion-dollar investment bonanza that’s betting on AI evolving at breakneck speed.

“Risks remain tilted to the downside,” the IMF said in its report. “A correction in AI-related investment or asset valuations could weigh disproportionately on Asia given its central role in global technology supply chains.”

Growth in emerging Asian markets and developing economies is expected to slow to 5.1% this year from 5.6% in 2025, before easing further to 4.9% in 2027, the fund said. Advanced economies in the region, meanwhile, are projected to expand 3.2% in 2026, up from 2.5% last year, before moderating to 2% in 2027.

See also: Germany to push EU to impose caps on more Chinese imports

The technology boom has also fuelled a rally in Asian equities, with valuations of regional technology stocks rising faster than their US counterparts this year. The IMF warned that elevated valuations, growing investor leverage and market concentration could increase the risk of significant turbulence.

Other risks cited by the report include a prolonged conflict in the Middle East that could keep energy prices elevated, rising global sovereign bond yields and a severe El Niño episode that could disrupt agriculture, fisheries and hydropower generation, adding to food and energy inflation.

title: TSMC results face high bar to calm global AI stock trade jitters
article:
(Oct 15): With strong earnings from global chip majors failing to boost the AI trade, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co faces a high bar to impress investors.

The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index has shed more than US$1.5 trillion in market value over the past six sessions on concerns over interest rates, financing for the AI buildout and the longevity of the chip cycle. TSMC shares fell as much as 2.8% in early Thursday trading in Taipei, ahead of its detailed earnings report due after the close.

TSMC, the world’s largest foundry, has already reported a 51% surge in quarterly sales. Still, solid recent results from Samsung Electronics Co and ASML Holding NV have done little calm market anxiety over chip shares.

“The bar is very high,” said Kevin Net, a portfolio manager at Financiere de L Echiquier. “To get a positive share price reaction, I think we need more than just a beat.” He’s looking for high margins and capital spending from TSMC, as well as signals of strong demand for AI and high-performance computing.

TSMC touched a record high earlier this month, among the first chip stocks globally to refresh its high after the July rout. It has been outperforming peers in the past few months thanks to its dominant position in outsourced manufacturing of processors needed to power the continued flood of new AI agents from major tech firms like Meta Platforms Inc.

See also: Apple unveils US$299 HomeView Hub as part of new smart home push

Yet it got caught up in the broader pullback in chip shares over the past week amid concerns over AI funding. Against this backdrop, TSMC’s results and guidance will be scrutinised to validate the sector’s growth narrative.

“The key readacross is whether TSMC turns more bullish on the duration and scale of AI demand,” said James Ooi, market strategist at Tiger Brokers. A bump in management’s AI accelerator revenue forecast or detail on the size of the gap in supply and demand for advanced chipmaking would be welcomed, he said.

See also: ASML’s guidance key to instill confidence in fragile chip trade

Consensus estimates have been climbing for the Taiwanese foundry’s 2027 capital spending, which is seen as a key metric for its share price. Goldman Sachs Group Inc now targets US$85 billion and UBS Group AG sees US$90 billion, compared with the US$75 billion average of firms polled by Bloomberg.

“Capex remains the utmost focus, as the company will likely continue to publicly state it remains committed to fulfilling backlogged customer demand,” JPMorgan Chase & Co’s sales desk wrote in a note to clients this week.

Another critical test is how well TSMC can protect its margins as it ramps up spending. Analysts estimate its gross margin at 66.5% for the three months through September, near the top of the company’s guidance range even if down slightly from the record level posted for the previous quarter.

“We are seeing a very long lasting cycle compared to historical standard, which is positive,” said Christophe Leroy, co-CIO and head of investment services at CBH Bank. “But at some point, we will see a cyclicality in the margin and you have to take into consideration what justify the current valuation.”

Investors will also closely parse TSMC’s commentary for indications of the impact from power grid constraints, regulatory hurdles or localised resistance to data centre construction.

“The market needs the whole AI ecosystem to work so if TSMC can demonstrate not only the demand is strong, but also the execution is also as planned,” said Xiadong Bao, a fund manager at Edmond de Rothschild Asset Management. For the AI capex narrative to continue, TSMC should continue to deliver on agentic AI promise, get strong commitments from hyperscalers and better manage bottlenecks, he added.

title: Exporter dollar sales bolster Malaysian ringgit, analysts say
article:
(Oct 15): Malaysian exporters are likely increasing conversions of their foreign-currency earnings into the ringgit, which stands to boost the local exchange rate through the rest of the year, analysts say.

Malaysia’s foreign-currency deposits fell 8.6% to RM308 billion ($96.9 billion) in August, the sharpest monthly decline since 2010, according to most recent central bank data. The drop indicates that exporters, benefitting from semiconductor shipments, may be converting those earnings into ringgit.

While September trade figures are scheduled for release next week, BNP Paribas SA expects ongoing corporate conversions to support the ringgit. That momentum, combined with robust economic fundamentals and foreign direct investment inflows, should help lift the currency to 3.90 per dollar by June 2027 from around 4.08 currently, according to the bank.

“We expect corporate conversion flows to rise from onshore exporters seeking to reduce the rising foreign exchange exposure and from foreign direct investment inflows such as for the construction of data centres,” said Parisha Saimbi, an emerging-market Asian foreign exchange and rates strategist at the bank.

Foreign investments have poured into Malaysia, which has become a major Asian hub for semiconductor manufacturing and data centres. Malaysia’s exports rose 45% in August from a year earlier, matching the growth seen in June, which was the fastest since August 2022.

See also: Rupee’s relentless slide draws importers into RBI currency fight

That has offered support for the ringgit, which rallied 1.5% against the dollar in August. Despite giving back some gains the following month amid a broader dollar rebound, it remains Southeast Asia’s best-performing currency this year behind the Singapore dollar.

Official efforts are reinforcing those market flows. Bank Negara Malaysia reiterated last month that it continues to encourage state-linked and private firms to repatriate and convert foreign-currency income. The strategy mirrors a similar move in South Korea, where officials urged exporters to repatriate overseas funds before the won began to recover.

With no official data on Malaysian exporter conversion of foreign currency proceeds into the ringgit, the size of business foreign-currency deposits held by commercial banks give an indication of such trends, according to Khoon Goh, the head of Asian research at Australia and New Zealand Banking Group.

See also: Billionaire Kotak says India should let rupee find its own level

“Since July there has been a fall in business foreign-currency deposits, which may point to increased conversion,” said Goh. “If there is a more noticeable rise in conversions, that should support the ringgit, though portfolio flows is also another important driver.”

title: ECB may not have to do as much if markets tighten, Dolenc says
article:
(Oct 15): A tightening in financial conditions may limit the need for European Central Bank monetary policy action, according to Governing Council member Primoz Dolenc.

“We’ve seen quite a bit of repricing in the markets,” Dolenc told Bloomberg Television in Bangkok, where he’s attending the International Monetary Fund’s annual meetings. “If there is a tightening on the financial market, then maybe we don’t have to do as much as we would otherwise.”

After two hikes, policymakers are debating how much further interest rates will have to rise to return an inflation rate approaching 4% back to their target. Price pressures turned out stronger than expected in September, while the economy has proven more resilient than thought.

Economists are anticipating a final move in December, which would take the deposit rate to 2.75% — a level estimated by some to start restraining economic activity.

Asked about that prospect, Dolenc said that the ECB is “approaching the restrictive area — probably we are still not there, but we are on the limits.”

Governing Council members Pierre Wunsch and Gediminas Simkus — from Belgium and Lithuania, respectively — both highlighted the latest inflation data when arguing in separate Bloomberg interviews that more tightening will probably be needed. While a move in December would be based on more data, action this month can’t be excluded, the latter said.

See also: Germany to push EU to impose caps on more Chinese imports

“We have the situation that second-round effects are not visible or not visible yet,” Dolenc said, echoing similar comments from Simkus and ECB president Christine Lagarde earlier this week.

Any decision will be complicated by investor concerns about the fiscal situation in France and other highly indebted members of the 21-nation euro zone. The country led a recent bond-market selloff that propelled the 10-year yield to highs not seen in almost a quarter century.

Bank of France governor Emmanuel Moulin argued that higher sovereign borrowing costs are putting pressure on financial conditions, potentially damping demand — as well as inflation.

See also: Canada aims for India trade deal by year-end, minister says

Meantime, economists and investors are speculating how much worse the market situation needs to get before the ECB would be willing to step in.

“We have different monetary policy measures in our toolkit, even TPI,” Dolenc said. “They will be used or they would be used if necessary if the conditions are met. It’s really difficult to speculate right now when, how, and why different kind of tools will be used.”

Lagarde, a Frenchwoman herself, put the ball in the court of President Emmanuel Macron’s government, encouraging politicians to work on reducing a deficit that’s spiralled to nearly twice the ceiling allowed by European rules. But she also told a group of finance ministers recently that the ECB has the instruments to deal with the situation if needed.

Rising government borrowing costs across developed economies in Europe, America and elsewhere are a major theme at the Bangkok gathering of global finance officials. IMF chief Kristalina Georgieva called on policymakers last week to take urgent action to reduce high debts and budget deficits.

title: Stock sell-off extends to Asia as chip rout deepens
article:
(Oct 15): A sell-off in global equities spread to Asia on Thursday morning as losses in chip stocks deepened after faster-than-expected US inflation fuelled bets that the Federal Reserve (Fed) will need to raise interest rates further. Treasuries rallied on haven demand.

MSCI Inc’s Asia-Pacific equities gauge slid 2.2%, heading for its lowest level since July. South Korea’s Kospi Index — a bellwether for artificial intelligence (AI) investments — led regional losses with a 7% drop as chipmakers Samsung Electronics Co and SK Hynix Inc both sank more than 8%.

Tech sentiment remained weak, with Nasdaq 100 Index futures falling 0.8%. Asian losses followed a slide on Wall Street that pushed the Russell 2000 Index into a correction, while a closely watched gauge of US semiconductor stocks had its longest daily losing streak since May 2025.

The fastest US inflation in five months prompted traders to ramp up bets on further Fed tightening, raising the prospect of additional rate hikes, even if policymakers pause in October. While Treasuries initially sank after the data was announced, they recovered most of the losses on appetite for bond yields near multi-year highs. The dollar weakened.

Stubborn US inflation, fuelled by elevated oil prices since the Middle East war broke out, is raising the prospect of more aggressive Fed tightening. At the same time, equity markets are coming under pressure after a blistering rally in AI-related stocks, bringing the US market’s longest stretch of tranquility since before the Covid-19 pandemic to an end.

See also: Asian stocks rise on signal Fed may not need aggressive rate hikes

“Inflation fear has been the main character recently,” said Anna Wu, an investment strategist and founder of Floodlines Research. “With inflation moving the rate path upward, it hurts everything else.”

Treasuries extended their gains at the start of Asian trading as the sell-off in equities spurred demand for haven assets. Yields on benchmark 10-year notes fell six basis points to 5.12%, while those on policy-sensitive two-year securities slid seven basis points to 4.73%.

Gold recovered after three days of declines to trade at about US$4,140 ($5,307) an ounce. While global crude oil benchmark Brent fell 1.1% to US$104.94 a barrel, elevated fuel prices were a factor in pushing up the US September consumer price index.

See also: ICE plans futures for livestock in a bid to challenge CME Group

Fed chairman Kevin Warsh has vowed not to steer markets with his own near-term outlook for monetary policy. But the inflation surprise will heighten scrutiny of his remarks late Thursday New York time in Bangkok, where he is scheduled to appear in a fireside chat with International Monetary Fund managing director Kristalina Georgieva.

Markets now price about 40 basis points of Fed hikes by the end of January, with the odds of an October move also edging up.

“It’s clear as ever that inflation is stubborn and moving in the wrong direction,” said Skyler Weinand at Regan Capital. “While we expect the Fed to pause on any rate changes in October, we expect rate hikes to resume in December.”

Market attention remains firmly on tech after CoreWeave Inc shares plunged as much as 17% on Wednesday. Its debt due in 2032, which investors bought at par four months ago, traded at less than 78 cents on the dollar.

Also, Anthropic PBC told prospective investors its third-quarter revenue hit US$16.8 billion, according to people familiar with the matter, as the AI model maker pushes ahead with plans to go public.

“The US CPI (consumer price index) surprise and CoreWeave bond sell-off are prompting investors to reassess financing risks across the AI sector,” said Jung In Yun, the chief executive officer of Fibonacci Asset Management Global.

title: Malaysia's IOI Properties Group eyes US$760 mil property deals in Singapore
article:
(Oct 15): Malaysian property tycoon Lee Yeow Seng is making waves as one of the most aggressive buyers of commercial real estate in Singapore, and he’s not done yet.

His IOI Properties Group Bhd is in exclusive talks and due diligence to purchase two property assets — Chijmes, a retail venue inside a former Catholic convent in its civic district, and the nearby Capitol Kempinski hotel, chief executive officer Lee said in an interview. He declined to disclose how much a final agreement will value the two assets at, citing ongoing negotiations.

Singapore developer Perennial Holdings has been trying to sell the Kempinski hotel, which was being marketed for about $600 million (US$468 million), according to people familiar with the matter. Chijmes was valued at $379 million at the end of 2025.

IOI’s debt-fueled buying spree has spurred a record year for real estate deals in Singapore. The firm is now courting investors for a new fund to ease the burden and give room for further expansion, as Lee seeks to challenge the wealthy clans that dominate the country’s property market.

“I’m a latecomer and I want to catch up with the rest,” the 47-year-old CEO said on the sidelines of a Forbes event in Singapore last week. “Most of them don’t share the vision of me.”

See also: Hongkong Land to seek stake in tycoon Ong Beng Seng’s Singapore assets — Bloomberg

Perennial controls about a third of Chijmes, and about 80% of Capitol Singapore, a broader complex that contains the hotel, as well as a retail mall and residential units. A vehicle backed by an unnamed Southeast Asian sovereign wealth fund has a minority stake in both assets, corporate records show. Other Chijmes investors include local food chain Breadtalk Group Pte Ltd and Ronald Ooi, the former chair and CEO of Kim Eng, a stock brokerage.

Representatives of Perennial, which is backed by investors including palm oil tycoon Kuok Khoon Hong and Chinese private equity veteran Fang Fenglei, didn’t respond to requests for comments.

IOI is in talks to bring high-end fashion brands into Chijmes to raise rents, which have been depressed by a predominance of food and beverage outlets, said Lee. It also wants a global ultra-luxury hotel brand to replace the Kempinski, he said.

See also: Singapore property investment sales hit $42.2 bil in 9M2026, surpassing 2025: Knight Frank

Lee’s Malaysia-listed firm, which has a large presence in its home country including one of the world’s largest malls, has splashed out on a range of Singapore properties in recent years. It gained full control of South Beach, an office complex that also houses his luxury penthouse and the JW Marriott hotel, after buying the majority stake from partner City Developments Ltd, which was looking to reduce debt. More recently, it bought office building Asia Square Tower 2, ballooning his commercial portfolio to $10 billion.

It’s also looking to form a joint venture with CapitaLand Investment Ltd, a property manager backed by Temasek Holdings Pte Ltd, to buy One Raffles Place, people familiar with the matter said in August. The iconic office complex is majority-owned by OUE REIT, which confirmed last week that it’s in exclusive discussions with the firms on a potential sale.

IOI’s rapid acquisitions have fuelled a surge in its borrowings, with its net debt rising to 85% of equity as of end-June. In 2024, its board rebuffed a proposal by Lee to acquire Shenton House in Singapore, amid concerns about heavy capital commitments in Singapore and Malaysia. Lee, who is a scion of a wealthy palm oil family in Malaysia, made the purchase on his own.

The firm eventually agreed to acquire the office building and its liabilities this month to redevelop it. Even with a planned Malaysia real estate investment trust listing, that’s expected to raise the firm’s gearing further. Lee said he aims to reduce the net debt to 30%-50% of its equity in the next three to five years.

His plans largely hinge on the success of a private fund, which Lee said will be set up in two months. He’s tapped ex-Pimco Prime Real Estate executive Varun Singh to oversee the vehicle, which will initially include two assets totalling $6 billion: the office portion of South Beach and the firm’s marquee office building IOI Central Boulevard Towers, whose tenants include Morgan Stanley and Jane Street Capital LLC.

Lee said the fund has courted investors including private equity firms, sovereign wealth funds and insurers, but declined to share names. It’s targeting an internal rate of return of 10%-11%, with semiannual distributions, he said.

To stay ahead of Singapore and the region’s corporate and economic trends, click here for Latest Section

The firm is looking to pare down its stake in the assets to about half, by marketing minimum holdings of about $500 million with a five to seven-year lockup. It will look to inject more of its Singapore assets into the fund during that period, and eventually list it as a REIT.

Lee is more optimistic about real estate prospects in Singapore than rival financial hub Hong Kong, saying the former doesn’t have the baggage of being fully absorbed back into China in 2047 and will continue to be favored by the wealthy and global companies.

Still, other bets in Singapore have stumbled, including IOI’s plans to build a city center luxury residential project with 683 homes. The firm is liable to pay a higher tax, having sold only about 15 units there. Lee said he has secured a short-term reprieve from Singapore authorities to next April and will keep appealing against paying the charge.

The firm is pivoting toward renting out its units to expats, he said, blaming a 60% levy imposed on most foreigner purchases in 2023 for the poor sales.

But he remains undeterred in investing in Singapore, saying lenders and the company’s board remains supportive. “If I can expand, why should I hold myself back?” he said. “No one has asked me to slow down.”

title: Oil holds gain as Middle East and Russia strikes threaten supply
article:
(Oct 15): Oil held a gain on Thursday as a flare-up in attacks from Russia to the Middle East threatened supply that only recently recovered to near pre-war levels.

West Texas Intermediate (WTI) held near US$95 ($122) a barrel, after rising 1% on Wednesday. Brent settled around US$106. A cargo ship sank after being struck by “unknown projectiles” as it transited the Strait of Hormuz, while Iran-backed Houthis continued to launch missile and drone attacks across Saudi Arabia.

Meanwhile, Russia accused Ukraine of attacking two oil refineries on Wednesday, flouting an “energy ceasefire” promoted by US President Donald Trump. Kyiv denied the claim, which Bloomberg couldn’t independently verify.

Brent has surged more than 70% this year as the US-Iran war roils energy markets. The depletion of stocks during the fighting has left global observed inventories 509 million barrels below pre-conflict levels, and on-land stockpiles near their lowest in at least a decade, the International Energy Agency said Wednesday, warning that supplies of diesel and other fuels will remain under pressure next year.

“If new attacks on oil infrastructure in the Middle East further disrupt petroleum supply in an already very tight physical market, energy costs and inflation would move even higher,” said Bart Melek, the global head of commodity strategy at TD Securities.

Russia’s Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said Ukrainian drones targeted refineries in the Saratov and Ryazan regions, Interfax reported. Ryazan, near Moscow, has a processing capacity of about 400,000 barrels a day and is among the largest oil refineries in the nation.

See also: Oil rises as Middle East attacks increase uncertainty over flows

In the Middle East, a growing number of oil tankers are avoiding areas where they would normally collect crude, suggesting increased Iranian attacks on shipping are complicating export logistics. Vessels capable of carrying at least 37 million barrels have stopped or changed course while heading toward loading areas off the United Arab Emirates (UAE) and Oman, though there’s no clear evidence yet that Gulf flows have declined.

Prospects for a diplomatic easing of tensions remain uncertain. Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said the Islamic Republic’s aims aren’t “endless war" or prolonged talks, but that it seeks to “wear down the enemy so that it is forced to accept our demands”.

Meanwhile, oil production in the UAE climbed to record levels last month, according to the IEA. The former Opec member has been one of the most successful regional producers in restoring flows through the Strait of Hormuz.

See also: Trump’s diesel deal irks allies and is unlikely to reduce prices

In the US, the industry-funded American Petroleum Institute reported nationwide crude inventories fell 11.1 million barrels last week, according to a document seen by Bloomberg. If confirmed by official data on Thursday, that would be the biggest drop since June 2025.
• WTI for November delivery slipped 0.3% to US$94.77 a barrel at 7.13am in Singapore on Thursday.
• Brent for December gained 0.4% to settle at US$106.06 a barrel on Wednesday.

title: US stocks fall on inflation woes as chip rout deepens
article:
(Oct 15): Stocks fell the most since July as a sell-off in chipmakers on Wednesday extended a decline that was fuelled by wagers the US Federal Reserve (Fed) will keep lifting interest rates to fight inflation.

The broad upswing in consumer prices reinforced bets on rate hikes even if the Fed pauses in October. The S&P 500 snapped its longest streak without a 1% drop in over six years. The Russell 2000 entered a correction. A gauge of chip giants sank 4.3%. CoreWeave Inc’s bonds hit levels that usually signal distress. Its chief said the market is acting “irrationally”.

A closely watched measure of semiconductor powerhouses such as Nvidia Corp and Broadcom Inc extended a six-day drop to about 12% amid mounting concerns about higher rates, lofty valuations and the massive cost of building artificial-intelligence (AI) infrastructure.

“While increased competition within AI, rising financing requirements, and higher rates may periodically add to volatility, we view this latest bout as more of a recalibration of expectations than a fundamental break in the AI investment story,” said Ulrike Hoffmann-Burchardi at UBS Chief Investment Office.

The equity retreat kindled investor demand for bonds with yields near multi-year highs. The latest inflation data had earlier triggered a plunge in Treasuries, prompting traders to briefly price in two Fed hikes by the end of January. Those bets faded. The dollar hit the highest since May 2025.

See also: Stocks bounce from lows on Williams’ rate remarks

“It’s clear as ever that inflation is stubborn and moving in the wrong direction,” said Skyler Weinand at Regan Capital. “While we expect the Fed to pause on any rate changes in October, we expect rate hikes to resume in December.”

Fed chairman Kevin Warsh has vowed not to steer markets with his own near-term outlook for monetary policy. But the inflation surprise will heighten scrutiny of his remarks late Thursday New York time in Bangkok, where he is scheduled to appear in a fireside chat with International Monetary Fund managing director Kristalina Georgieva.

Inflation pressures are broadening beyond energy, suggesting the last mile back to target could remain bumpy and keep rates elevated, according to Jeff Roach at LPL Financial. The latest report complicates the Fed’s decision this month as the road back to price stability is looking increasingly difficult to navigate, he added.

See also: S&P 500 holds firm as banks report earnings, chipmakers slump

The question is whether firmer core inflation is enough to alter the Fed’s path, according to Seema Shah at Principal Asset Management. Markets are clearly unsettled, but the latest report is not strong enough to revive the case for an October hike, she said.

While the latest consumer price index raises concerns around inflation risks, the Fed has already communicated a gradual hiking process, according to TD Securities’ strategists including Oscar Munoz and Gennadiy Goldberg.

“Today’s report makes the chance of an October hike higher, but we still believe the Fed will hold and opt for December as the market is already doing some of the work for them,” they said.
